shipped.warum: In October 1884 a company in Edinburgh contracted for 47,000 acres on Sarasota Bay, “below the frost line”. In the same year a vigilance committee of settlers killed Harrison T. Riley and the postmaster Charles E. Abbe; Florida's courts convicted its leaders. In December 1885 Scottish colonists landed; in January snow fell, and by February the colony had broken up.
shipped.quelle: The Economist 1884; Florida Reports 1886 and 1888; The Pensacolian and The Atlanta Constitution 1885; Chicago Daily Tribune 1886; Florida gazetteer 1886–87; Time (London) 1887; Grismer (1946).

shipped.warum: After the colony the company built the town it had drawn in Edinburgh: a wharf, a rooming house and the De Soto Hotel. The work ended and weeds grew in Main Street; a railroad came in 1892, the freezes of 1894–95 hit the groves less than elsewhere, and in 1902 fifty-three voters made the village a town.

After the railroad, the patrons: Bertha Palmer of Chicago bought up to 100,000 acres from 1910, John and Charles Ringling bought on the bay from 1911 and promised to advertise Sarasota on their circus posters. The town became a city in 1913 with a mill of tax for advertising. Two Black men were lynched in Manatee County; Newtown was begun about 1914.
shipped.quelle: Chicago Sunday Tribune 1910; Manatee River Journal 1910–1919; NAACP 1919; Grismer (1946).

shipped.warum: In 1921 Sarasota became the seat of its own county, in a year of a mob with a rope, a Black prisoner killed at a convict camp and a hurricane on the bayfront. In the boom of 1925–26 booklets promised twenty-five thousand residents, John Ringling's causeway opened the keys, the Klan paraded and advertised, and Newtown argued whether to belong to the city.
shipped.quelle: Manatee River Journal 1921; Monthly Weather Review 1921; booklets of about 1922 and 1924; Sarasota Herald 1925–26; Grismer (1946).

shipped.warum: After 1926 most of the boom's fortunes and four banks were gone, and the city and county owed more than thirteen million dollars. The circus came for the winter, a museum and an art school opened, celery was grown on drained muck by Black labourers, trailer tourists filled Payne Park, and federal relief built Myakka River State Park, an auditorium and a beach casino.
shipped.quelle: Grismer (1946); census 1930; ship-canal hearings 1937; Myakka Rattler 1935; NYA directory 1936.
shipped.zk: Bust · Circus and museum · Celery and trailers · Relief

planned.warum: From 1942 an Army air base stood east of the town, with more than 3,000 men at its peak; it closed on 2 January 1946. In the same year Karl H. Grismer published The Story of Sarasota: the history a town tells about itself, and what it leaves out.
planned.quelle: Florida newspapers 1942–45; USGS Sarasota quadrangle 1944; Grismer (1946).

missing.warum: The town's own weekly is not digitized. A survey of 1995 lists two issues at the University of South Florida and a run from 1910 to 1924 with the city's historical resources department. Until it can be read, the apparatus relies on the newspaper of Bradentown and on papers elsewhere.

missing.kurz: The bust in its own record
missing.warum: The digitized Sarasota Herald ends in August 1926. The collapse, the hurricane of September 1926, the bank failures and the town's debts are told in module 5 only from Grismer's history of 1946. The Herald of 1926–1938 (catalogued at the University of Florida but not online), the records of the bondholders' settlement and Florida's banking reports would be needed.

missing.kurz: The colony in the Scottish press
missing.warum: The company's pamphlet of 1885 and the Scottish newspapers that reported the colonists' complaints (the North British Mail, January 1886) are not reachable here; the British Newspaper Archive is paid. They are known through American reprints.
The colonist's memoirs were lent to Grismer as a family manuscript. Only the passages Grismer printed in 1946 are used; a part printed in 1999 is protected.

missing.kurz: The prisoner killed at Salt Springs, 1921
missing.warum: The Manatee River Journal of 23 June 1921 reports that a former convict guard, J. R. Bunkley, was held for the murder of a Black prisoner at Salt Springs and bound over to the grand jury of Sarasota County (printed in module 4). The prisoner is not named, and the outcome — indictment, trial, verdict — has not been found. The county's court records and Florida's reports on its convict camps of 1921–22 would be needed.
No public-domain source before 1946 has been found on who was allowed on Sarasota's beaches. Later reports (1955–56) are named only as pointers.

The Sarasota Herald of 1925–26 records William Selby and his wife as winter residents from Marietta, Ohio. Their arrival, their house on the bay and the gardens that bear Marie Selby's name lie outside what the sources read so far can carry; a chapter of its own is left open.
The Ringling museum (opened 1931) and the art school are documented here only in passing. The painters, classes and exhibitions of the 1930s and 1940s are left open for a chapter of their own.
The Federal Writers' Project guide has a long entry on Sarasota, but its copyright was renewed in 1967. It is not quoted here.

The colonist John Lawrie of Paisley wrote the letter of complaint that the New-York Tribune printed in January 1886 and the Scottish papers copied. The New York paper is on Chronicling America, which is not reachable here; a summary in the Los Angeles Times of 17 January 1886 is too worn in the scan to be read reliably.

missing.kurz: Harrison T. Riley and Charles E. Abbe
missing.warum: Both murdered men appear in the sources only through their killers, the courts and the press. What Riley was accused of comes from the committee itself; why Abbe was hated is disputed in the press of 1885. A genealogy of the Abbe family (1916) and the post office records have not yet been read against the page image.
missing.quelle: Abbe-Abbey Genealogy (1916); records of the Post Office Department.

missing.warum: The Supreme Court's opinions affirm the judgments but do not state the sentences, and what became of the convicted men — pardons, commutations, escapes — is not documented in the sources read so far. The records of the Florida Board of Pardons and the state prison would be needed.

The Calusa, the Cuban and Spanish fishing ranchos on the bay, the Seminole wars and the Whitakers' settlement of the 1840s are told here only in passing. The federal documents on the fishing ranchos of the 1830s and the naval records of the Civil War on the bay have been found but not yet read against the page image.
missing.quelle: Congressional documents of the 1830s; Official Records of the Union and Confederate Navies, vol. 17 (1903).

missing.warum: The act of the Florida legislature of 1921 that created the county has not yet been read at its source; the apparatus prints the boundary as the Bradentown paper reported it.

The digitized papers of the boom were written by and for white Sarasota. No Black newspaper, church record or letter from Newtown in the 1920s has been found in a public-domain source; the quarter speaks here only through police notes and announcements.

missing.kurz: The Black school and church before 1914
missing.warum: A teacher for a Black school at Sarasota is listed in 1894; where the school stood, who attended it, and the Black churches of the village before Newtown have not been found in the public-domain sources read. The county school board's minutes would be the next source.
missing.quelle: Manatee County Board of Public Instruction, minutes.

missing.kurz: The village in the gazetteers of the 1890s
missing.warum: The Florida railroad gazetteer of 1895 lists Sarasota with a population of 100, the De Soto Hotel and J. H. Gillespie as justice of the peace (OCR only); it has not yet been read against the page image.

Both lynchings are printed here only from the NAACP's list of 1919. The reports of the county paper and of the Tampa press, which would tell what happened and who took part, have not yet been read against the page image.
missing.quelle: Manatee River Journal, March 1903 and July 1912.

missing.warum: The act of the Florida legislature granting the charter has not been read at its source; its clause on advertising is quoted from Grismer.

The Bradentown city directory of 1916 includes Sarasota and marks each resident as white or coloured; counted, it would show where Black and white residents lived and worked. It has not yet been read through.

Grismer counts those employed in the celery crop in the 1940s as “70 per cent … negroes”. Their wages, housing and camps in the 1920s and 1930s, and any labour dispute, have not been found in public-domain sources.
missing.quelle: To be found (farm labour reports, Florida Department of Agriculture).

missing.kurz: Who served in the CCC at Myakka
missing.warum: Company 1421's paper names its enrollees but nowhere states their colour. Whether Black young men served at Myakka, in this company or another, has not been found in the sources read.
missing.quelle: Florida CCC records; Myakka Rattler, full run.
